cty.london.m.0.t: The Romans lay out Londinium as a civilian town about four years after the invasion of AD 43, at the lowest bridging point of the Thames.
cty.london.m.1.t: Around AD 60 the Iceni under Boudica destroy the young settlement; it is rebuilt and becomes the provincial capital.
cty.london.m.2.t: Between about 180 and 225 the Romans build the London Wall: roughly 3 km long, 6 m high and 2.5 m thick, the line the medieval city will keep.
cty.london.m.3.t: William the Conqueror’s stone keep, the first stone castle in England, is begun about 1078 and largely finished by 1088.
cty.london.m.4.t: The first stone bridge, begun in 1176, is completed in 1209 and carries houses and shops across the river for six hundred years.
cty.london.m.5.t: The plague reaches London in the autumn of 1348 and peaks until May 1349; the city loses at least half of its population.
cty.london.m.6.t: In Henry VIII’s reign London’s population reaches 100,000; by 1605 it is about 225,000 and the largest city in the kingdom by far.
cty.london.m.7.t: The last great plague kills about 60,000 to 70,000 Londoners, roughly a fifth of the city.
cty.london.m.8.t: From 2 to 5 September a fire that begins in Pudding Lane destroys about 60 per cent of the city, more than 13,000 buildings, Old St Paul’s and 87 parish churches, with few recorded deaths.
cty.london.m.9.t: The new cathedral is topped out in 1708 and Parliament declares it complete on 25 December 1711; its dome stands over a city rebuilt in brick.
cty.london.m.10.t: The first census counts 1,114,644 people in Greater London; the city grows from about a million in 1800 to 6.7 million a century later.
cty.london.m.11.t: The London and Greenwich Railway, the first steam line in the capital, opens on 8 February 1836; Euston, the first mainline terminus, follows in 1837.
cty.london.m.12.t: The Metropolitan Railway, the first underground line in the world, opens in 1863, in the same years that Bazalgette lays more than 2,100 km of sewers after the Great Stink of 1858.
cty.london.m.13.t: German bombing from 7 September 1940 to 10 May 1941 opens a campaign that kills just under 30,000 Londoners by the end of the war.
cty.london.m.14.t: Coal smoke trapped over the city in December 1952 kills an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 people and leads to the Clean Air Act.
cty.london.m.15.t: Renzo Piano’s glass spire at London Bridge is inaugurated on 5 July 2012, three weeks before the Olympic Games open in Stratford.
cty.new-york.m.0.t: When Henry Hudson sails the Half Moon into Upper New York Bay on 2 September 1609, some thousands of Lenape live in about 80 settlements around the harbour; Verrazzano had seen the bay in 1524.
cty.new-york.m.1.t: The Dutch West India Company founds New Amsterdam in 1624; Fort Amsterdam is begun about 1626 and the town is incorporated in 1653.
cty.new-york.m.2.t: Four English frigates arrive in August 1664; Stuyvesant surrenders and the town is renamed New York after the Duke of York.
cty.new-york.m.3.t: On 21 September 1776 a fire destroys about 1,000 houses, a quarter of the city, at the start of a British occupation that lasts until 25 November 1783.
cty.new-york.m.4.t: Washington is inaugurated on 30 April 1789 and New York is the first capital under the Constitution, until the government moves to Philadelphia in 1790.
cty.new-york.m.5.t: The Commissioners’ Plan of 1811 lays the Manhattan street grid from 14th Street to Washington Heights.
cty.new-york.m.6.t: The canal opens in 1825 and makes the port the gateway to the interior; the city, 96,373 people in 1810, counts 166,136 by 1825.
cty.new-york.m.7.t: The park, the first landscape park in an American city, opens in 1858 after a design competition the year before.
cty.new-york.m.8.t: The city reaches a million people in 1872 (942,292 in 1870, 1,206,299 in 1880).
cty.new-york.m.9.t: The bridge opens on 24 May 1883 and joins Brooklyn to Manhattan across the East River.
cty.new-york.m.10.t: On 1 January 1898 the city is consolidated with Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island; the census of 1900 counts 3,437,202.
cty.new-york.m.11.t: The Interborough Rapid Transit company opens the first subway line in 1904, while the first skyscrapers reshape the skyline.
cty.new-york.m.12.t: The Chrysler Building of 1930 and the Empire State Building of 1931 crown the Art Deco skyline of the Depression years.
cty.new-york.m.13.t: The twin towers are completed on 4 April 1973, two years before the fiscal crisis of 1975.
cty.new-york.m.14.t: The attack on the World Trade Center kills 2,976 people in the towers and on the ground.
cty.new-york.m.15.t: The new tower, the tallest in the Western Hemisphere by architectural height, opens on 3 November 2014.
cty.seoul.m.0.t: In 18 BC the kingdom of Baekje founds its capital Wiryeseong, believed to lie within modern Seoul; it stays the royal seat until 475.
cty.seoul.m.1.t: King Sukjong of Goryeo builds a palace near the later Gyeongbokgung and names the town Namgyeong, the Southern Capital.
cty.seoul.m.2.t: Yi Seong-gye chooses Hanyang in September 1394 and moves the capital from Kaesong; construction begins in October.
cty.seoul.m.3.t: The main palace Gyeongbokgung and the royal ancestral shrine Jongmyo are built as the dynasty’s first works.
cty.seoul.m.4.t: Taejo’s wall around the city, launched in 1395 and largely complete with its eight gates in 1396, is rebuilt in stone under Sejong and restored by Sukjong in 1704.
cty.seoul.m.5.t: The second palace, Changdeokgung, is built east of the main palace.
cty.seoul.m.6.t: In April 1592 the city is taken by the Japanese forces of Hideyoshi’s invasion.
cty.seoul.m.7.t: In the years of the Korean Empire the first streetcar lines are laid and a railway links the capital to Incheon; the wall is breached for the tram lines.
cty.seoul.m.8.t: After the annexation treaty of 1910 Japan renames the city Gyeongseong, Keijō in Japanese, and demotes it to the rank of other cities of Gyeonggi province.
cty.seoul.m.9.t: The first post-liberation census counts 1,446,019 people.
cty.seoul.m.10.t: The city falls to the North on 28 June 1950 as the Han River bridge is blown; it changes hands four times, and at least 191,000 buildings lie in ruins afterwards.
cty.seoul.m.11.t: Two expansions in 1963 raise the city’s area from about 268 to 613 square kilometres and take in Gangnam south of the river.
cty.seoul.m.12.t: The Seoul Metropolitan Subway begins operating in 1974; Line 1 replaces the Jongno streetcar.
cty.seoul.m.13.t: Seoul hosts the Asian Games of 1986 and the Summer Olympics of 1988; the 63 Building of 1985 marks the new skyline of Yeouido.
cty.seoul.m.14.t: The census of 1990 counts 10,612,577 people, the city’s peak.
cty.seoul.m.15.t: The stream buried under an elevated road is uncovered and restored in 2005, three years after the city hosts the opening of the World Cup.
cty.tokyo.m.0.t: Ōta Dōkan builds a castle at Edo from 1457 on the site of the present Imperial Palace’s East Garden.
cty.tokyo.m.1.t: When Tokugawa Ieyasu first enters Edo in 1590 he finds a small fortified residence and no real town.
cty.tokyo.m.2.t: Ieyasu is appointed shogun in 1603 and sets up his headquarters at Edo Castle; Nihonbashi bridge is built the same year as the starting point of the highways.
cty.tokyo.m.3.t: The fire of 2 March 1657 burns a vast part of the city and kills about 100,000 people.
cty.tokyo.m.4.n: The largest city in the world
cty.tokyo.m.4.t: The first census of 1721 counts about 1.3 million people; Edo had passed 500,000 in the 1650s and is by many estimates the largest city on earth.
cty.tokyo.m.5.t: The earthquake of 11 November 1855, magnitude 6.9 to 7.0, kills 8,000 to 10,000 people.
cty.tokyo.m.6.t: With the fall of the shogunate the city is renamed Tokyo in July 1868, and the emperor moves there in 1869; an estimated 360,000 daimyo retainers leave the city.
cty.tokyo.m.7.n: The railway and the Ginza brick town
cty.tokyo.m.7.t: A railway opens between Shinagawa and Yokohama in October 1872 and is extended to Shinbashi; after a fire the same year Ginza is rebuilt in brick to a design by Thomas Waters.
cty.tokyo.m.8.t: The earthquake of 1 September 1923 kills two to three per cent of a population of 4.5 million and leaves two million homeless.
cty.tokyo.m.9.t: The Tokyo Underground Railway begins operating between Asakusa and Ueno in 1927.
cty.tokyo.m.10.t: The raid of 9–10 March 1945 kills 90,000 to 100,000 people in a few hours and destroys a quarter of the city’s buildings.
cty.tokyo.m.11.t: The Tōkaidō Shinkansen begins operating and the Summer Olympics are held in October 1964; the population passes ten million the following year.
cty.tokyo.m.12.t: The broadcasting tower Skytree is completed in 2012.
cty.tokyo.m.13.t: Chosen in 2013 to host the 2020 Games, the city holds them in 2021 after the pandemic postponement.
cty.st-petersburg.m.0.t: Peter the Great founds the city on 27 May 1703; the Peter and Paul Fortress on Hare Island is its first building.
cty.st-petersburg.m.1.t: Peter moves the capital from Moscow to Saint Petersburg in 1712.
cty.st-petersburg.m.2.t: The Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences is established in 1724; the Kunstkamera is built by 1727.
cty.st-petersburg.m.3.t: Rastrelli’s Winter Palace is completed in 1762; the Hermitage collection is founded in 1764.
cty.st-petersburg.m.4.t: Falconet’s equestrian statue of Peter is unveiled in 1782.
cty.st-petersburg.m.5.t: The death of Alexander I is followed by the Decembrist revolt in Senate Square in December 1825.
cty.st-petersburg.m.6.t: The Moscow–Saint Petersburg railway begins operating in 1851.
cty.st-petersburg.m.7.t: Montferrand’s St Isaac’s Cathedral is completed in 1858.
cty.st-petersburg.m.8.t: The census of 1897 counts 1,267,023 people; by 1900 the city is the fourth largest in Europe.
cty.st-petersburg.m.9.t: The shooting of petitioners in January 1905 begins the revolution of 1905, which spreads from the city to the provinces.
cty.st-petersburg.m.10.t: The city is renamed Petrograd on the outbreak of the war in 1914.
cty.st-petersburg.m.11.t: The February Revolution ends the monarchy and the October Revolution overthrows the Provisional Government; some two million people leave the city in the following years.
cty.st-petersburg.m.12.t: On 24 January 1924, three days after Lenin’s death, Petrograd is renamed Leningrad.
cty.st-petersburg.m.13.t: From 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944 the city is besieged; more than a million civilians die.
cty.st-petersburg.m.14.t: The Leningrad Metro opens in 1955 with stations in marble and bronze.
cty.st-petersburg.m.15.t: A referendum on 12 June 1991 restores the original name, in force from 6 September.
cty.moscow.m.0.t: Moscow is first recorded in 1147 as the place where Yuri Dolgoruky met Sviatoslav Olgovich.
cty.moscow.m.1.t: The town is destroyed by the Mongols in the winter of 1237–38.
cty.moscow.m.2.t: The seat of the Metropolitan of Rus is moved to Moscow, which rises over the other principalities.
cty.moscow.m.3.t: The Kremlin citadel is founded in stone in 1367; it withstands sieges, including that of 1382.
cty.moscow.m.4.t: The Dormition Cathedral is built in the Kremlin in 1479 by Aristotele Fioravanti.
cty.moscow.m.5.t: Italian architects invited by Ivan III in the 1480s, among them Pietro Antonio Solari, build the Kremlin walls as they now stand, completed in 1495.
cty.moscow.m.6.t: Moscow has about 100,000 people by 1500, 45,000 houses in 1520, and roughly doubles to 200,000 in the first half of the seventeenth century.
cty.moscow.m.7.t: The Cathedral of the Intercession on the Moat, St Basil’s, is built on Red Square around 1560.
cty.moscow.m.8.t: In 1571 the Crimean Tatars burn the city; the annals say only 30,000 of 200,000 inhabitants survive.
cty.moscow.m.9.t: The militia of Minin and Pozharsky drives the Polish–Lithuanian garrison from the city.
cty.moscow.m.10.t: Plague in 1771 is followed in September by a riot in which the crowd kills the archbishop.
cty.moscow.m.11.t: When Napoleon enters in September 1812 the city burns; about three-quarters of it lies in ruins.
cty.moscow.m.12.t: The 645 km railway to Saint Petersburg begins operating in 1851.
cty.moscow.m.13.t: The city counts 1,023,817 people in 1900, having grown from 250,000 in 1812.
cty.moscow.m.14.t: Lenin moves the capital back to Moscow on 12 March 1918.
cty.moscow.m.15.t: The Moscow Metro opens on 15 May 1935; the city grows from one to ten million in the century.
cty.rome.m.0.t: By tradition recorded in Livy, Romulus founds the city in 753 BC.
cty.rome.m.1.n: The Gallic sack and the Servian Wall
cty.rome.m.1.t: The Gauls sack Rome after the battle of the Allia; the Servian Wall is rebuilt about 380 BC.
cty.rome.m.2.n: The Appian Way and the first aqueduct
cty.rome.m.2.t: The Via Appia and the Aqua Appia are built in 312 BC.
cty.rome.m.3.t: The fire of AD 64 destroys much of the city; rumour blames Nero, Nero blames the Christians.
cty.rome.m.4.t: Work on the Flavian Amphitheatre begins in AD 72.
cty.rome.m.5.t: Hadrian rebuilds the Pantheon about 125 in the form it keeps.
cty.rome.m.6.t: Construction of the Aurelian Wall begins in 270.
cty.rome.m.7.t: Constantine’s basilica over the apostle’s tomb is built about 320.
cty.rome.m.8.t: Alaric’s Visigoths sack Rome in 410; Genseric’s Vandals follow in 455.
cty.rome.m.9.t: Charlemagne is crowned Roman emperor in St Peter’s on Christmas Day 800.
cty.rome.m.10.t: Boniface VIII proclaims the first Holy Year; nine years later the papacy moves to Avignon and returns only in 1377.
cty.rome.m.11.t: Julius II begins the new basilica in 1506; it is completed in 1626.
cty.rome.m.12.t: The troops of Charles V loot and ruin the city in 1527.
cty.rome.m.13.t: Construction of the new St Peter’s Basilica is completed in 1626.
cty.rome.m.14.t: Italian troops take Rome in 1870 and it becomes the capital of the kingdom.
cty.rome.m.15.t: Rome hosts the Summer Olympics of 1960, fifteen years after its liberation in 1944.
cty.istanbul.m.0.t: Greek colonists found Byzantium on the point between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara in 657 BC.
cty.istanbul.m.1.t: Constantine renames the city in 324, dedicates it as his capital in 328 and his column in May 330; the population is some 20,000 in 324 and 200,000 by 393.
cty.istanbul.m.2.t: The land walls of Theodosius II are built in 413.
cty.istanbul.m.3.t: Begun after the Nika riots of 532, Justinian’s church is completed on 26 December 537; the city holds 300,000 to 500,000 people.
cty.istanbul.m.4.t: The plague of 541 kills about 40 per cent of the population.
cty.istanbul.m.5.t: The city withstands sieges in 674–678 and 717–718.
cty.istanbul.m.6.t: In April 1204 the crusaders take and thoroughly sack the city; it is recovered in 1261 with only about 35,000 people.
cty.istanbul.m.7.t: After a siege from 6 April, Mehmed II takes the city on 29 May 1453 and moves his capital here from Edirne.
cty.istanbul.m.8.t: The Grand Bazaar is built about 1460 and the Topkapı Palace begun in 1465; the Fatih Mosque follows in 1470.
cty.istanbul.m.9.t: Sinan’s mosque for Suleiman is completed in 1557.
cty.istanbul.m.10.t: The Blue Mosque is completed in 1616.
cty.istanbul.m.11.t: The first bridge across the Golden Horn is built in 1845.
cty.istanbul.m.12.t: Sirkeci railway station opens on 27 July 1872; the Orient Express from Paris begins running in 1883.
cty.istanbul.m.13.t: On 13 October 1923 the capital moves to Ankara; the city is renamed Istanbul in 1930.
cty.istanbul.m.14.t: The city counts 1,000,022 people in 1950, having reached 1,125,000 in 1914 before the losses of the war years.
cty.istanbul.m.15.t: The first bridge between Europe and Asia opens on 19 April 1973.
cty.paris.m.0.t: The Parisii, settled on the Seine since about 250 BC, are defeated by Labienus in 52 BC and the Roman town of Lutetia is laid out on the left bank.
cty.paris.m.1.t: Clovis makes Paris his capital in 508.
cty.paris.m.2.t: The Vikings besiege the city for a year in 885–886.
cty.paris.m.3.t: Construction of the new cathedral begins in 1163; the altar is consecrated in 1182.
cty.paris.m.4.n: Philip Augustus’s wall and the Louvre
cty.paris.m.4.t: Philip Augustus orders the first wall around the whole city in 1190 and builds the Louvre fortress between 1190 and 1202.
cty.paris.m.5.t: Innocent III charters the University of Paris in 1215; the Sorbonne opens in 1257.
cty.paris.m.6.t: Louis IX’s chapel for the Crown of Thorns is consecrated on 26 April 1248.
cty.paris.m.7.t: With about 200,000 people in 1328 Paris is the most populous city in Europe; the Black Death of 1348–49 kills 40,000 to 50,000.
cty.paris.m.8.t: On 24 August 1572 the bells of Saint-Germain l’Auxerrois signal the massacre of Protestants; about two thousand die by 30 August.
cty.paris.m.9.t: The Pont Neuf, begun in 1578, is finished between 1600 and 1607, the first bridge in the city without houses.
cty.paris.m.10.t: On 6 May 1682 the seat of the monarchy moves from the Tuileries to Versailles.
cty.paris.m.11.t: On 14 July 1789 the crowd storms the Bastille.
cty.paris.m.12.t: The cholera epidemic of 1832 kills about 18,500 to 20,000 people between March and October.
cty.paris.m.13.t: Napoleon III and his prefect Haussmann begin the reconstruction of the centre in 1853; the city has about a million people and annexes its suburbs in 1860.
cty.paris.m.14.t: After the Prussian siege of 1870–71 the Commune is crushed in the Bloody Week of 21–28 May 1871, with thousands of Communards killed.
cty.paris.m.15.n: The Eiffel Tower and the Métro
cty.paris.m.15.t: The 300-metre tower opens on 2 April 1889 for the Exposition; the first Métro line follows on 19 July 1900, and the population stands at 2,715,000 in 1901.
cty.venice.m.0.t: By a much later tradition the city is founded on 25 March 421; modern scholars do not accept the account.
cty.venice.m.1.t: After Pepin’s failed invasion of 810, Rialto comes to prominence over the other lagoon settlements and becomes Venice proper.
cty.venice.m.2.t: Mark the Evangelist is designated patron of the city in 828.
cty.venice.m.4.t: After the sack of Constantinople monuments and works of art are carried to Venice.
cty.venice.m.5.n: The closing of the Great Council
cty.venice.m.5.t: The Serrata of 1297 fixes the ruling families.
cty.venice.m.6.t: The Black Death strikes the city in 1348.
cty.venice.m.7.t: A printing press is in operation in 1469; Aldus follows in the 1490s.
cty.venice.m.8.t: The census of 1548 counts 158,069 people, the city near its peak.
cty.venice.m.10.t: The wooden bridge of 1173 is replaced in stone in 1591.
cty.venice.m.11.t: The Italian plague of 1629–31 strikes Venice.
cty.venice.m.12.t: The Republic falls in 1797 and a Provisional Municipality is set up under the French.
cty.venice.m.13.t: The Milan–Venice railway begins operating in 1842, bringing the mainland to the lagoon.
cty.venice.m.14.t: The first Venice Biennale opens on 30 April 1895.
cty.venice.m.15.t: On 4 November 1966 the highest acqua alta on record floods the city.
cty.florence.m.0.t: A Roman colony is founded about 59 BC.
cty.florence.m.1.t: The commune is adopted and the Republic of Florence established in 1115–16.
cty.florence.m.2.t: The mint is established and the gold florin introduced in 1252.
cty.florence.m.3.t: The third ring of walls is built in 1284.
cty.florence.m.4.t: Construction of the Palazzo Vecchio begins in 1299.
cty.florence.m.5.t: The Ponte Vecchio is rebuilt in 1345.
cty.florence.m.6.t: The plague strikes the city in 1348.
cty.florence.m.7.t: The revolt of the wool-workers runs from 1378 to 1382.
cty.florence.m.8.t: Cosimo comes to power on 6 October 1434.
cty.florence.m.9.t: The dome of Santa Maria del Fiore is completed and the cathedral consecrated in 1436.
cty.florence.m.10.t: Piero II flees before Charles VIII and the Republic is restored; Savonarola is executed on 23 May 1498.
cty.florence.m.11.t: The siege of Florence begins on 24 October 1529.
cty.florence.m.12.t: Vasari begins the Uffizi in 1560; it is finished in 1581.
cty.florence.m.13.t: The capital of Italy moves from Turin to Florence in 1865; the census of 1861 counts 150,864 people.
cty.florence.m.14.t: On 4 November 1966 the Arno floods the city.
cty.vienna.m.0.t: Vindobona is settled about AD 100; the first mention of Vienna by name comes in 881.
cty.vienna.m.1.t: Henry II of Austria makes Vienna his capital in 1155.
cty.vienna.m.2.t: St Stephen’s is built from about 1160; the tower is rebuilt in the 1860s.
cty.vienna.m.3.t: The University of Vienna is founded in 1365.
cty.vienna.m.5.t: The great plague of Vienna strikes in 1679.
cty.vienna.m.6.t: The second Ottoman siege ends with the battle of 1683.
cty.vienna.m.7.t: The city has 150,000 people in 1724 and 200,000 by 1790.
cty.vienna.m.9.t: The walls come down and the Ring Road is built from 1858; the Opera opens in 1869 and the World Exposition is held in 1873.
cty.vienna.m.11.t: The giant wheel of the Prater is erected in 1897.
cty.vienna.m.12.t: The population reaches 2,031,000 in 1910, its peak.
cty.vienna.m.14.t: Germany annexes Austria in 1938; the Vienna Offensive of 1945 ends the war in the city.
cty.vienna.m.15.t: The Vienna International Centre opens in 1979, three years after the U-Bahn.
cty.jerusalem.m.0.t: The earliest settlement near the Gihon Spring dates to 4500–3500 BC; the name appears in Egyptian execration texts about 2000 BC.
cty.jerusalem.m.1.t: David captures the city about 1010 BC and makes it his capital.
cty.jerusalem.m.2.t: Solomon builds the First Temple about 962 BC.
cty.jerusalem.m.3.t: In 587–586 BC the Babylonians destroy the city and the First Temple.
cty.jerusalem.m.4.t: The Second Temple is completed in 516 BC, in the sixth year of Darius.
cty.jerusalem.m.5.t: Herod expands the Temple Mount and rebuilds the Temple from 19 BC.
cty.jerusalem.m.6.t: Titus ends the main phase of the Jewish war and destroys Herod’s Temple in AD 70; Hadrian refounds the city as Aelia Capitolina in 136.
cty.jerusalem.m.7.t: After Helena’s visit in 326 the first Church of the Holy Sepulchre is built in 335.
cty.jerusalem.m.8.t: Caliph Umar takes the city in 636–637, after the Persian sack of 614.
cty.jerusalem.m.9.t: Abd al-Malik builds the Dome of the Rock between 687 and 691.
cty.jerusalem.m.10.t: The First Crusade takes the city in 1099 and slaughters much of its Muslim and Jewish population.
cty.jerusalem.m.11.t: Saladin takes the city from the Crusaders in 1187.
cty.jerusalem.m.12.t: Suleiman the Magnificent rebuilds the walls between 1535 and 1538.
cty.jerusalem.m.13.t: General Allenby enters Jerusalem on foot in December 1917, weeks after the Balfour Declaration; the British Mandate follows in 1920.
cty.jerusalem.m.14.t: The war of 1948 divides the city; West Jerusalem is proclaimed Israeli territory in July and the east is annexed by Jordan in 1950.
cty.jerusalem.m.15.t: Israeli forces take the Old City on 7 June 1967 and declare the city unified on 28 June.
cty.athens.m.0.t: Solon’s laws are established in 594 BC.
cty.athens.m.1.t: The Persians burn the city in 480 and 479 BC.
cty.athens.m.2.t: Construction of the Parthenon begins in 447 BC.
cty.athens.m.3.n: The Peloponnesian War and the plague
cty.athens.m.3.t: The war with Sparta begins in 431 BC; the plague strikes in 430.
cty.athens.m.4.t: Athens is defeated in the Peloponnesian War in 404 BC.
cty.athens.m.5.t: Roman forces sack the city in the 80s BC.
cty.athens.m.6.t: The Agora is sacked by the Heruli in 267.
cty.athens.m.7.t: The Ottomans take the city in 1456.
cty.athens.m.8.t: The Venetians under Morosini besiege the city in 1687.
cty.athens.m.9.t: The marbles are taken to Britain from 1801.
cty.athens.m.10.t: Athens becomes the capital of the kingdom in 1834; the university is founded in 1837.
cty.athens.m.11.t: The Games of 1896 are held in the city.
cty.athens.m.12.t: More than a million Greek refugees from Asia Minor settle in and around Athens; the metropolis counts 802,000 by 1928.
cty.athens.m.14.t: Clashes in December 1944 open the road to civil war.
cty.athens.m.15.t: The Summer Olympics and Paralympics are held in 2004, with the metro extended in 2000.
cty.alexandria.m.0.t: Alexander renames the village of Rhacotis Alexandria about 331 BC.
cty.alexandria.m.1.t: Ptolemy proclaims himself king in 305 BC.
cty.alexandria.m.3.t: The lighthouse is built about 247 BC.
cty.alexandria.m.4.t: Caesar takes the city in 48 BC and the great library burns.
cty.alexandria.m.5.t: After the battle of 30 BC Antony and Cleopatra die and Augustus takes the city.
cty.alexandria.m.6.t: Theodosius orders the destruction of the pagan temples in 391; Hypatia is lynched in 415.
cty.alexandria.m.7.t: The Arabs take the city in 641–642 and move the capital to Fustat.
cty.alexandria.m.8.t: Earthquakes in 1303 and 1323 bring down the lighthouse.
cty.alexandria.m.9.t: The French take the city in 1798; the British in 1801. By 1800 only about 8,000 people live there.
cty.alexandria.m.10.t: The canal to the Nile is built in 1819 and the port revives.
cty.alexandria.m.11.t: The Cairo–Alexandria railway begins operating in 1856.
cty.alexandria.m.12.t: The city counts 60,000 in 1840 and 170,000 by 1863.
cty.alexandria.m.13.t: The city counts 919,024 in 1947 and about 1.5 million by 1965.
cty.alexandria.m.14.t: The new library is inaugurated in 2002.
cty.baghdad.m.0.t: Al-Mansur begins the Round City in 762.
cty.baghdad.m.1.t: Harun al-Rashid comes to power in 786.
cty.baghdad.m.2.t: The civil war between al-Amin and al-Ma’mun ends in a siege of the city.
cty.baghdad.m.3.t: The caliphate moves to Samarra in 836 and returns in 892.
cty.baghdad.m.4.t: The Seljuks take power in 1055; the Nizamiyya college is founded in 1067.
cty.baghdad.m.5.t: The Mustansiriya madrasa is founded in 1232.
cty.baghdad.m.6.t: In January–February 1258 Hulagu’s forces destroy the city and kill most of its population.
cty.baghdad.m.7.t: Timur captures the city again in 1401.
cty.baghdad.m.8.t: The city becomes the capital of the Ottoman eyalet of Baghdad in 1535; the Safavids hold it from 1623 until Murad IV retakes it in 1638.
cty.baghdad.m.10.t: The city is estimated at 100,000 people in 1895.
cty.baghdad.m.11.t: The British take the city in March 1917; it becomes the capital of the Mandate in 1920.
cty.baghdad.m.12.t: The coup of 14 July 1958 ends the monarchy; the city is capital of the Republic.
cty.baghdad.m.14.t: The bombing of 1991 includes the Amiriyah shelter on 13 February.
cty.baghdad.m.15.t: The battle of Baghdad is fought on 3–12 April 2003.
cty.cairo.m.0.t: The mosque of Amr ibn al-As is built in 642 at Fustat, the first Muslim capital of Egypt.
cty.cairo.m.1.t: Ahmad ibn Tulun founds al-Qata’i in 873 and his mosque is built in 879.
cty.cairo.m.2.t: The Fatimid caliph al-Mu’izz founds Misr al-Qahira in 970; al-Azhar is established the same year.
cty.cairo.m.3.t: The city wall and the gates, among them Bab Zuwayla and Bab al-Nasr, are built in 1092.
cty.cairo.m.5.t: The city becomes the capital of the Mamluk Sultanate in 1250.
cty.cairo.m.6.t: Ottoman forces take Cairo in 1517 and it becomes a provincial capital.
cty.cairo.m.7.t: Napoleon arrives in 1798; the city has about 200,000 people in 1800.
cty.cairo.m.8.t: The mosque on the Citadel is built in 1848.
cty.cairo.m.9.t: The railway station is built in 1856.
cty.cairo.m.10.t: The opera house opens in 1869 for the Suez Canal celebrations, in Ismail’s new quarters.
cty.cairo.m.11.t: The census of 1947 counts 2,090,654 people (654,476 in 1907).
cty.cairo.m.12.t: The fire of January 1952 burns the European quarter; Ismailia Square is renamed Tahrir.
cty.cairo.m.14.t: Line 1 of the Cairo Metro begins operating in 1987.
cty.cairo.m.15.t: The uprising against the Mubarak regime begins on 25 January 2011.
cty.beijing.m.0.t: The city government dates the grants of Ji and Yan by King Wu of Zhou to 1045 BC.
cty.beijing.m.1.t: The Liao rename Youzhou Nanjing, the Southern Capital, in 938; 22,000 people live inside the walls.
cty.beijing.m.2.t: The Jin move their capital here in 1153 and name it Zhongdu, the Central Capital.
cty.beijing.m.3.t: After a long siege the city surrenders in 1215 and is looted and burned.
cty.beijing.m.4.t: Kublai Khan begins Dadu in 1267 and names it capital of the Yuan in 1271; the city counts 952,000 by 1327.
cty.beijing.m.5.t: Xu Da captures Dadu in 1368 and it is renamed Beiping.
cty.beijing.m.6.t: The Yongle Emperor builds the Forbidden City from 1406 to 1420 and moves the capital from Nanjing in 1421.
cty.beijing.m.7.t: The Outer City wall is built in 1553.
cty.beijing.m.8.t: On 3 May 1644 the Manchus seize Beijing.
cty.beijing.m.9.t: Anglo-French forces take the city and Lord Elgin orders the Old Summer Palace burned.
cty.beijing.m.10.t: Boxers and Qing troops besiege the Legation Quarter in June 1900; foreign armies lift the siege and occupy the city.
cty.beijing.m.11.t: Students gather in Tiananmen Square on 4 May 1919; in 1928 the capital moves to Nanjing and the city is renamed Beiping.
cty.beijing.m.12.t: Mao proclaims the People’s Republic from Tiananmen Gate on 1 October 1949; the city has just over two million people.
cty.beijing.m.13.t: The Ming walls are demolished in the 1960s for the subway, which begins trial operation in 1969, and the 2nd Ring Road.
cty.beijing.m.14.t: The protests of spring 1989 end in the military crackdown of 3–4 June.
cty.beijing.m.15.t: The Games open on 8 August 2008 at the National Stadium; the city counts 13.56 million in 2000 and 20.18 million by 2011.
cty.kyoto.m.0.t: Emperor Kanmu arrives on 22 October 794 and names the city Heian-kyō on 8 November; it is laid out on the grid of Chang’an, 4.5 by 5.2 km, without walls.
cty.kyoto.m.1.t: The East and West temples on the southern edge are the only temples permitted within the city.
cty.kyoto.m.2.t: The Golden Pavilion is founded in 1397.
cty.kyoto.m.3.t: The war of 1467–77 burns almost half the city, which does not fully recover until the mid-sixteenth century.
cty.kyoto.m.4.t: In the late sixteenth century Hideyoshi lays out new streets and raises the earthwork walls called odoi.
cty.kyoto.m.5.t: The great Kyoto fire of 1788 destroys most of the city.
cty.kyoto.m.6.t: The fighting of 1864 burns down 28,000 houses.
cty.kyoto.m.7.t: The imperial court moves to Tokyo in 1869; the modern city is formed on 1 April 1889 with 279,165 people.
cty.kyoto.m.9.t: The canal, begun in 1885, is completed on 9 April 1890.
cty.kyoto.m.10.t: Kyoto introduces the country’s first commercial electric railway, powered by the canal, and builds the Heian Shrine for the city’s eleven-hundredth anniversary.
cty.kyoto.m.11.t: The population exceeds one million in 1932.
cty.kyoto.m.12.t: Removed from the atomic target list and largely spared from bombing, the city keeps its temples.
cty.kyoto.m.14.t: The city hosts the conference that produces the protocol on greenhouse gases, and the new Kyoto Station opens.
cty.delhi.m.0.t: Anangpal Tomar founds Lal Kot in 1052; the Chauhans take it in 1180 and rename it Qila Rai Pithora.
cty.delhi.m.1.t: Muhammad Ghori defeats Prithviraj at Tarain in 1192 and sacks the city; the Qutb Minar is begun.
cty.delhi.m.2.t: From 1206 Delhi is the capital of the Sultanate under Qutb-ud-din Aibak.
cty.delhi.m.3.t: Timur enters the city on 18 December 1398; it is sacked and left in ruins.
cty.delhi.m.4.t: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 and founds the Mughal dynasty.
cty.delhi.m.5.t: Shah Jahan moves the capital back to Delhi and builds the walled city with the Red Fort; it becomes the capital in 1648.
cty.delhi.m.6.t: Nadir Shah sacks the city and a two-day massacre kills over 30,000.
cty.delhi.m.7.t: The Company defeats the Marathas at the battle of Delhi in 1803.
cty.delhi.m.8.t: British forces besiege the city from 8 June 1857 and take it on 21 September; the last Mughal is exiled.
cty.delhi.m.9.t: At the Durbar of 1911 George V announces the move of the capital from Calcutta.
cty.delhi.m.10.t: Lutyens’ New Delhi is inaugurated in 1931.
cty.delhi.m.11.t: About 500,000 Hindu and Sikh refugees come to Delhi and about 300,000 Muslims leave for Pakistan.
cty.delhi.m.12.t: The Delhi Metro begins operation in 2002.
cty.delhi.m.13.t: Delhi hosts the Games in 2010; the census of 2011 counts 16,753,235 people.
cty.mexico-city.m.0.t: The Mexica found the island city about 1325 where, in the legend, an eagle with a snake perches on a cactus.
cty.mexico-city.m.1.t: The empire is formed in 1428; the Templo Mayor to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc rises at its centre.
cty.mexico-city.m.2.n: The largest city in the Americas
cty.mexico-city.m.2.t: Causeways and two aqueducts from Chapultepec serve a city of more than 200,000 fed by chinampas.
cty.mexico-city.m.4.t: After a siege from 22 May the city falls on 13 August 1521 and is rebuilt as the Spanish capital.
cty.mexico-city.m.5.t: The Royal and Pontifical University is founded in the early 1550s.
cty.mexico-city.m.6.t: Construction of the cathedral starts in 1573 and is completed in 1813.
cty.mexico-city.m.7.t: Rains inundate the capital in 1629 and the waters remain for years.
cty.mexico-city.m.8.t: In 1692 a crowd burns the viceroy’s palace.
cty.mexico-city.m.10.t: The Army of the Three Guarantees enters the city on 21 September 1821.
cty.mexico-city.m.11.t: US forces take the city in September 1847; French troops occupy it in 1863.
cty.mexico-city.m.12.t: The palace, begun under Díaz, is inaugurated in 1934.
cty.mexico-city.m.13.t: The massacre of 2 October 1968 precedes the Games by ten days; the Metro opens in 1969.
cty.mexico-city.m.14.t: The earthquake of 19 September 1985 devastates the centre.
cty.mexico-city.m.15.t: The city proper counts 9,209,944 people in 2020, from 2,233,709 in 1950.
cty.cusco.m.0.t: The Killke people occupy the valley from 900 to 1200 and build the first fortress at Sacsayhuamán about 1100.
cty.cusco.m.1.t: By legend Manco Cápac founds the city in the twelfth century; the Inca expand Sacsayhuamán in the thirteenth.
cty.cusco.m.2.t: Pachacuti, who comes to power in 1438, is credited with the city’s design in the shape of a puma, Sacsayhuamán at its head.
cty.cusco.m.3.t: Pizarro takes possession of the city on 15 November 1533.
cty.cusco.m.4.t: The city is re-established on 23 March 1534 with its first alcaldes.
cty.cusco.m.5.t: Manco Inca besieges the city from May 1536; the fight for Sacsayhuamán is fought on 14 May.
cty.cusco.m.6.t: The Iglesia del Triunfo is built in 1539; the basilica is built from 1560 and consecrated in the eighteenth century.
cty.cusco.m.7.t: The earthquake of 31 March 1650 destroys almost all the colonial buildings.
cty.cusco.m.8.t: The rebellion besieges the city in 1781; its leader is executed in the Plaza de Armas.
cty.cusco.m.9.t: Independence is proclaimed in Cusco on 3 August 1814; Pumacahua is executed in 1815.
cty.cusco.m.10.t: The city has 47,000 people in the 1840s.
cty.cusco.m.11.t: The earthquake of 21 May 1950 damages more than a third of the city.
cty.cusco.m.12.t: UNESCO lists the City of Cusco in 1983.
cty.lima.m.0.t: Pizarro founds the Ciudad de los Reyes on 18 January 1535 and construction of the cathedral begins.
cty.lima.m.2.t: The university of San Marcos, the first in the city, is founded in 1551; the first printing press arrives in 1584.
cty.lima.m.4.t: The walls built in 1684–87 enclose a city that the earthquakes of October and December 1687 largely destroy.
cty.lima.m.5.t: The earthquake of 28 October 1746 severely damages the city and destroys Callao.
cty.lima.m.6.t: San Martín’s forces enter and independence is declared in 1821.
cty.lima.m.7.t: The Lima–Callao line is completed about 1850.
cty.lima.m.8.t: The city walls are torn down in the early 1870s.
cty.lima.m.10.t: Chilean troops occupy the city from 1881 to 1883.
cty.lima.m.11.t: An earthquake hits the city on 24 May 1940; the population is about 600,000.
cty.lima.m.13.t: The historic centre is listed by UNESCO in 1988.
cty.lagos.m.0.t: Rui de Sequeira names the lagoon for Portugal about 1472; the Awori settle the island of Eko.
cty.lagos.m.1.t: About 1600 the Oba of Benin appoints the Awori chief Ashipa ruler of Eko; tribute to Benin lasts until 1830.
cty.lagos.m.2.t: Akinsemoyin opens the kingdom to the slave trade in the 1760s; by the early nineteenth century Eko is the largest slave exporter in the northern hemisphere.
cty.lagos.m.3.t: Britain bombards Lagos in 1851, installs Akitoye and in 1852 signs a treaty abolishing the slave trade.
cty.lagos.m.4.t: Oba Dosunmu signs the Treaty of Cession on 6 August 1861; Lagos is declared a colony on 5 March 1862.
cty.lagos.m.5.t: Electric street lighting begins on 19 September 1898.
cty.lagos.m.6.t: The railway to Ibadan opens on 4 March 1901 and the Carter Bridge joins the island to the mainland.
cty.lagos.m.7.t: Lagos becomes the capital of the amalgamated Colony and Protectorate on 1 January 1914.
cty.lagos.m.8.t: The census of 1931 counts 126,474 people (98,303 in 1921).
cty.lagos.m.9.t: Lagos remains the capital when Nigeria becomes independent in 1960.
cty.lagos.m.10.t: Lagos State is created in 1967; the state capital moves to Ikeja in 1976.
cty.lagos.m.13.t: The federal government moves to Abuja in 1991.
cty.lagos.m.14.t: The urban agglomeration is estimated at 8,767,000 in 2005; Eko Atlantic begins in 2013.
